newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street opening hinges on June employment data.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street opening hinges on June employment data.

text.p: Wall Street's opening direction Thursday depends on whether U.S. employment data for June show signs of a significantly tighter labor market and wage inflation, analysts said.
The figures, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, are the final hurdle for financial markets this week, before a three-day holiday weekend in the United States.
U.S. bond and foreign exchange markets will close early today, at 1500 EDT/1900 GMT, and remain closed on Friday for the U.S. Independence Day holiday.
"The (stock) market will focus on the key economic number this month -- employment," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

Stocks and bonds are seen opening higher if the employment data come in within the range of forecasts, but markets could suffer if the data point to a lower jobless rate, higher wages and inflation, analysts said.

Analysts expect non-farm payrolls to rise by around 222,000, after an increase of 138,000 in May. The unemployment rate is expected to hold steady at 4.8 percent, and average hourly earnings are seen rising by 0.4 percent.
Ahead of the report, the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was off 0.25 point at 915.25, while the long bond was up 3/32 at a 6.70 percent yield.
On Wednesday, U.S. stocks roared higher after Federal Reserve policy makers left interest rates unchanged.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 73.05 points to 7795.38.
"If the employment data come in significantly above expectations today, expect to see the market sell off," said Hildegard Zagorski, an analyst at Prudential Securities.
Average hourly earnings will receive the most attention, according to Cardillo.
"Wages are the key," he said. "If they rise by more than 0.3 percent or 0.4 percent, the bond market could get hit and stocks should see pressure."
But analysts said volume would quickly thin out as traders left for the long weekend.
"We might not see the real fireworks in the market until Monday," Cardillo said. "A lot of traders are already gone."
Japan's Nikkei average closed down 75.01 at 20,121.41.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 47.4 points at 4798.8.
U.S. stocks trading in London were slightly higher in thin trade.
The dollar was off earlier lows against the yen in Tokyo, trading at 114.46/56 yen.
In Europe the dollar was off 40-month highs of 1.7566 marks and was trading at 1.7540/45 marks.
The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that index funds are stirring up overseas stock markets as they invest in foreign companies.
The New York Times said in its Market Place column that the Thai government's decision to devalue the currency represented a gamble to boost the country's economy.
((--Wall Street Desk 212-859-1730))
